alerts.title: DTG-associated hyperglycemia: pre-diabetes now present
alerts.message: Guidelines report hyperglycemia in non-diabetic adults on DTG, more common in those transitioned to DTG. Risk factors include age ≥30, family history of DM, hypertension, and BMI ≥25. This patient has three risk factors (age 36, family history, BMI 32.4) and was transitioned to DTG 18 months ago. She now has impaired fasting glucose (118 mg/dL) and HbA1c 6.1% (pre-diabetic range). Acanthosis nigricans confirms insulin resistance. Evidence for drug attribution: new-onset dysglycemia temporally following DTG initiation with multiple risk factors. Against: weight gain and family history may independently drive dysglycemia. Guidelines state those with ≥2 risk factors and high glucose should not transition to DTG; her fasting glucose now exceeds the threshold (>6.95 mmol/L = 125 mg/dL) cited for withholding DTG.

evidence.recommended_action: Assess whether DTG should be continued given pre-diabetes progression. Consider switching to EFV400 or ATV/r-based regimen per guidelines. Refer for diabetes management and lifestyle intervention.

alerts.title: Significant weight gain on DTG with metabolic complications
alerts.message: Guidelines identify rapid weight gain as a risk factor for diabetes in PLHIV and note DTG is associated with hyperglycemia. This patient gained 17 kg (65→82 kg) in 18 months on TLD, with BMI rising from 25.6 to 32.4 (overweight to obese). She also developed elevated BP (118/74→138/88), dyslipidemia (LDL 148, triglycerides 212, HDL 38), and acanthosis nigricans. This constellation strongly suggests DTG-associated metabolic syndrome. The weight gain itself compounds diabetes and cardiovascular risk. Non-drug causes (diet, sedentary lifestyle) should also be evaluated. No clinician plan was documented for this visit.

evidence.recommended_action: Evaluate for DTG contribution to weight gain and metabolic syndrome. Consider regimen switch and initiate weight management, dietary counseling, and cardiovascular risk reduction.

alerts.title: Missing quarterly glucose monitoring on DTG
alerts.message: Guidelines require blood glucose monitoring every 3 months for the first year in patients transitioned to DTG who have risk factors for hyperglycemia. This patient had multiple risk factors at transition (age ≥30, BMI ≥25, family history of DM) and should have had at least four glucose checks during the first 12 months. No prior glucose results are recorded since the baseline fasting glucose of 92 mg/dL at switch. The current HbA1c of 6.1% and fasting glucose of 118 mg/dL confirm dysglycemia has developed, but the absence of interim monitoring means progression was not detected earlier.

evidence.recommended_action: Establish regular glucose monitoring (at least every 3 months) given pre-diabetes. Repeat HbA1c in 3 months. Screen for diabetes complications per guidelines.

alerts.title: TDF renal monitoring overdue
alerts.message: Guidelines require serum creatinine and eGFR every 12 months for experienced patients on TDF. The patient has been on TDF-containing regimens for over 4 years total (3 years TDF/3TC/EFV, then 18 months TLD). Today's creatinine (0.9 mg/dL) is acceptable, but no eGFR was reported and no prior creatinine results are documented. Without trend data, renal function changes cannot be assessed. TDF nephrotoxicity can manifest as progressive renal impairment.

evidence.recommended_action: Calculate eGFR from today's creatinine. Ensure annual serum creatinine and eGFR monitoring is scheduled and documented going forward.
